content: Amlodipine is administered as part of the treatment regimen. It is currently unknown whether valsartan is excreted into human breast milk. However, valsartan has been shown to be excreted into the milk of lactating rats. It is important to note that drug levels in animal breast milk may not accurately reflect the levels in human breast milk. Given that many drugs are excreted into human breast milk and considering the potential for adverse reactions in nursing infants exposed to Exforge, a decision must be made to either discontinue nursing or discontinue the drug, taking into account the importance of the medication to the mother. In clinical studies, no overall differences in the efficacy or safety of Exforge were observed in patients aged 75 years or older. However, it is not possible to rule out the possibility of greater sensitivity to the drug in some elderly individuals. For amlodipine, clinical studies did not include a sufficient number of subjects aged 65 years and older to determine whether their response differs from that of younger patients. Other reported clinical experiences have not identified significant differences in responses between elderly and younger patients. In general, dose selection for elderly patients should be approached with caution, typically starting at the lower end of the dosing range. This reflects the higher likelihood of reduced hepatic, renal, or cardiac function, as well as the presence of concomitant diseases or other drug therapies. Elderly patients exhibit decreased clearance of amlodipine, leading to an increase in the area under the curve (AUC) by approximately 40% to 60%. Therefore, a lower initial dose may be required. For valsartan, no overall differences in efficacy or safety were observed in patients aged 75 years or older. However, as with amlodipine, the possibility of greater sensitivity in some elderly individuals cannot be excluded. There is no FDA guidance regarding the use of amlodipine besylate and valsartan in specific gender populations. Similarly, there is no FDA guidance on the use of these medications in specific racial populations. The safety and effectiveness of Exforge in patients with severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance <30 mL/min) have not been established. No dose adjustment is required for patients with mild (creatinine clearance 60–90 mL/min) or moderate (creatinine clearance 30–60 mL/min) renal impairment. For patients with hepatic impairment, exposure to amlodipine is increased. Therefore, lower doses of Exforge should be considered in these patients. For valsartan, no dose adjustment is necessary in patients with mild-to-moderate hepatic disease. However, no dosing recommendations can be provided for patients with severe liver disease. There is no FDA guidance on the use of amlodipine besylate and valsartan in women of reproductive potential or in males. Additionally, there is no FDA guidance on the use of these medications in immunocompromised patients. In terms of administration and monitoring, Exforge should be dosed once daily. The dosage may be increased after 1 to 2 weeks of therapy to a maximum of one 10/320 mg tablet once daily, as needed, to achieve blood pressure control.
